Paper explainer · arXiv 2611.06908 · Apple · 4 Nov 2026

HALO: humanoid home skills learned entirely in simulation

Hu et al., Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation. Short text; the diagrams and equations carry the explanation. Figures marked “Paper Fig.” are taken from the paper; the rest are redrawn from its text and tables.

What it does

A Unitree G1 takes a request like “crouch under the table, then sit on the chair” and does it in a home it has never seen, using only its own cameras and onboard computers.

The trick

Every training example is made in simulation: a motion diffusion model writes the movement, a procedural generator builds the room, a renderer makes the head-camera video. No teleoperation and no scan of the test room.

The stack

A VLM picks the next subtask (~0.5 Hz) → a VLM + diffusion generator turns the RGB image into a 5 s whole-body plan (~3 Hz) → a depth-aware RL tracker follows it on the motors (50 Hz).

Result

91% success over 360 real trials in 6 unseen rooms (6 skills). Chains of 2–3 skills: about 70%.

Part 1

Three layers, three speeds

The top two layers answer what to do (“which chair?”). The bottom layer answers how to do it physically (“where is the seat, really, and how do I keep balance on the way down?”).

OAK-1W (head)
120° RGB, 1280×800 at 30 fps → generator and orchestrator.
RealSense D435i
Points 55° down. IR dot projector turned off; the raw left/right IR pair goes into a small stereo network (LiteAnyStereo, 7.6M params) → clean 48×84 depth for the tracker.
Mac mini M4 Pro
64 GB, in a backpack. Runs both VLMs and the DiT. Generator ~152 ms per plan; orchestrator 0.72 s per decision (1.46 s when sharing the GPU).
Jetson Orin NX
Factory computer. Tracker in C++ on a real-time kernel, TensorRT, never blocks.
Part 2

The data engine: compute instead of people

An hour of teleoperated data costs at least an hour of human time. HALO makes each episode with no human: generate motion, drop it into a generated room, render what the head camera would see.

StepWhat happensNumbers
1 · MotionKIMODO (a motion diffusion model) makes several candidates per segment; forward-kinematics checks reject foot sliding, floor penetration, flying, joint-limit hits.SIT: 50,000 made, 77% pass, 25,349 kept
2 · RoomInfinigen builds living rooms, offices, bedrooms (3.5–9.5 m sides, 20–80 objects).1,200 → 1,178 finish → 1,000 train, 178 held out
3 · PlaceRotate + shift the whole episode (robot path and chair together) until nothing collides.pelvis ≥ 0.35 m from furniture
4 · RenderLighting is path-traced once per room and baked into textures, so any fast rasterizer can render it. Fisheye camera matched to the OAK-1W.13.2 s → 56–87 ms per frame
Filter · keep the best candidate
\[ \xi^\star=\arg\max_{n\le N}\,S(\xi_n),\qquad \text{“pass”} \iff \text{all hard checks OK} \;\wedge\; S(\xi_n)\ge 0.75 \]

\(\xi_n\) is a candidate motion, \(S\) a weighted score over forward-kinematics checks. SIT uses 33 checks (23 hard) and the best of 16 walks; CRAWL/CROUCH use 21 checks, threshold 0.65, best of 20.

Placement · first collision-free rigid move
\[ T^\star=\text{first } T=(x,y,\psi)\in \underbrace{\mathcal G_{10\,\text{cm}}}_{\le 800\text{ free cells}}\times\underbrace{\{0^\circ,15^\circ,\dots,345^\circ\}}_{24\text{ headings}} \;\text{ with }\; \min_{\tau}\,\operatorname{dist}\!\big(T\,p^{\text{pelvis}}_{\tau},\ \text{furniture}\big)\ge 0.35\,\text{m} \]

One \(T \in SE(2)\) moves the robot path and the target object together. At most 800 × 24 = 19,200 tries; the pelvis is checked every third frame.

Total corpus: 162,698 episodes, 296.3 h at 30 Hz, mean 6.6 s each, 10 fixed instructions (“sit arm chair”, “walk to box”, …).

Part 3

Motion generator: image + words → 5 s of motion

Output · one plan
\[ \hat q_\tau=\big[\,\hat\theta_\tau\,;\ \Delta\hat p_\tau\,;\ \Delta\hat r_\tau\,\big]\in\mathbb R^{29+3+4\,=\,36},\qquad \hat q_{t+1:t+H}\in\mathbb R^{150\times 36} \]

29 joint angles, pelvis shift (3) and pelvis rotation as a quaternion (4), all relative to the pelvis at time \(t\). H = 150 frames = 5 s at 30 Hz. Relative coordinates mean the plan does not depend on where the room is.

Training: flow matching with a fixed start

Eq. 1 · mix plan and noise
\[ x_s=s\,x_1+(1-s)\,x_0,\qquad x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\quad s\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1.5,\,1) \]

\(x_1\) is a clean (normalized) plan, \(x_0\) is noise, \(s\) is the flow time. \(s=0\) is pure noise, \(s=1\) is the plan. Beta(1.5, 1) has mean 0.6, so training sees more of the nearly clean end.

Eq. 2 · learn the velocity, but only after the prefix
\[ \mathcal L(\phi)=\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{1}{D\,(H-P)}\sum_{\tau=P+1}^{H}\big\|\,v_\phi(\tilde x_s,\tilde s,c)_\tau-(x_1-x_0)_\tau\big\|^2\right] \] \[ \tilde x_s=\big[\,x_{1,\;1:P}\;;\;x_{s,\;P+1:H}\,\big],\qquad \tilde s=\big[\,\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{P=15},\ \underbrace{s,\dots,s}_{H-P=135}\,\big] \]

The first P = 15 frames (0.5 s) are handed in clean and labelled “time = 1”. The loss scores only the other 135 frames (135 × 36 = 4,860 numbers). The network learns to continue whatever start it is given.

One joint value: clean \(x_1=0.8\), noise \(x_0=-0.4\), \(s=0.25\). Then \(x_s=0.25\cdot0.8+0.75\cdot(-0.4)=-0.1\). The target velocity is \(x_1-x_0=1.2\) for every \(s\). One Euler step of size 1/15 moves the value by \(1.2/15=0.08\).
On the robot · 15 Euler steps, prefix re-pinned each step
\[ x\;\leftarrow\;x+\tfrac{1}{15}\,v_\phi(x,\tilde s,c),\qquad x_{1:15}\;\leftarrow\;\text{next 15 frames of the plan being executed} \]

Start the last 135 frames from noise, step \(s\) from 0 to 1, and overwrite the first 15 frames after every step. The new plan therefore starts exactly where the current one is going.

Why the prefix: swapping plans without a jump

The robot cannot pause while the network thinks, so the next plan is computed while the current one runs. The swap must not jerk the reference.

Part 4

Motion tracker: follow the plan, using depth

The plan is only kinematic. It may put the seat 10 cm off or ignore a box’s weight. The tracker turns it into motor targets while seeing the real geometry through depth. Most prior trackers that follow generated motion are blind.

Eq. 3 · distillation
\[ \mathcal L_{\text{distill}}(\theta)=\mathbb E_{i,t}\Big\|\,\mu_\theta\big(o^{\text{stu}}_{i,t}\big)-\mu^{\text{teacher}}_{k(i)}\big(o^{\text{priv}}_{i,t}\big)\Big\|^2 \]

Env \(i\) runs skill \(k(i)\). The student sees only onboard sensors \(o^{\text{stu}}\); the expert for that skill sees privileged state \(o^{\text{priv}}\). The student matches the expert’s mean action.

Eq. 4 · per-skill advantage normalization
\[ \hat A_{i,t}=\frac{A_{i,t}-\mu_{k(i)}}{\sigma_{k(i)}+\varepsilon} \]

Each skill has its own critic and its own mean \(\mu_k\) and spread \(\sigma_k\) of advantages. Skills with big rewards (object terms) then cannot drown out locomotion in the shared actor’s gradient.

If SIT advantages have \(\sigma=6\) and walking advantages \(\sigma=0.5\), raw SIT gradients are ~12× larger. After dividing by each \(\sigma\), both have spread 1.
Rewards · tracking, object, safety (Table VII)
\[ r_{\text{pelvis}}=\exp\!\big(-\|e_{p,\text{pelvis}}\|^2/0.3^2\big),\qquad g_{\text{hand}}=\exp\!\big(-(d_{\text{hand}}/0.3)^2\big),\qquad r_{\text{obj}}=g_{\text{hand}}\,\exp\!\big(-\|e_{p,\text{obj}}\|^2/0.3^2\big) \] \[ r_{\text{knee}}=-10\sum_{j\,\in\,\text{knees}}\frac{\max\!\big(0,\,-\tau_j\dot q_j-150\big)^2}{500^2} \]

Six Gaussian kernels track pelvis and 14 body links (position, rotation, velocities). Copying the arm motion in the air would score well while the box stays put, so object rewards count only when a wrist is near the object (\(g_{\text{hand}}\)). The knee term punishes braking power above 150 W, which real motors cannot absorb in deep crouches.

Pelvis 0.1 m off → \(e^{-0.11}=0.89\); 0.3 m off → \(e^{-1}=0.37\). Hand 0.15 m from the box → \(g=e^{-0.25}=0.78\); 0.6 m away → \(g=e^{-4}=0.02\), so moving the box with a foot earns almost nothing. Knee braking 400 W → \((250/500)^2=0.25\) → reward −2.5.
Eq. 5 · PD gains from rotor inertia
\[ k_{p,j}=I_j\,\omega_n^2,\qquad k_{d,j}=2\zeta I_j\,\omega_n,\qquad \alpha_j=\frac{0.25\,\tau_{\max,j}}{k_{p,j}},\qquad q^{\text{tar}}_t=q_0+\alpha\odot a_t \]

Every joint gets the same natural frequency \(\omega_n=10\) Hz (62.8 rad/s) and damping ratio \(\zeta=2\). The action \(a_t\) is scaled so one unit asks for a quarter of the joint’s torque limit.

\(I=0.02\) kg·m² → \(k_p=0.02\cdot62.8^2=79\) N·m/rad, \(k_d=2\cdot2\cdot0.02\cdot62.8=5.0\) N·m·s/rad. With \(\tau_{\max}=88\) N·m, \(\alpha=22/79=0.28\) rad per unit action.
Depth input · same in sim and on the robot
\[ \tilde d=\log\!\big(1+\operatorname{clip}(d,\ 0.2,\ 2.5)\big) \]

0.2 m → 0.18, 1.0 m → 0.69, 2.5 m → 1.25. Holes in real depth are set to the far plane (2.5 m) so they never look like a close obstacle. The simulated depth camera also ray-casts the robot’s own arms and legs, so self-occlusion looks real.

Part 5

Orchestrator: a VLM supervising a checklist

Requests are vague (“sit down” names no chair) and hide steps (a table in the way means crouch first). An off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 4-bit, on the Mac mini) writes a plan of up to 8 subtasks as JSON, then watches the camera and moves the plan along. It is prompted, not trained.

Plan for one request

“Crouch under the table, then sit on the chair.”

  1. done crouch_under
  2. running go_to_chair
  3. pending sit

Each subtask sends one fixed text prompt to the generator, e.g. sit → “sit down on the chair”.

Each check, it calls one tool

complete_step
step done, move on
retry_step
stopped early, goal still ahead
insert_step
blocked; run another subtask first
set_plan
rewrite the plan
ask_operator
unsure or lost sight of the target
finish_mission
whole task done
Part 6

Results

Simulation tests run the full stack in MuJoCo, in real time, in 100 rooms never used for training. Real tests: 6 rooms never seen, scanned or mapped; 10 trials per task per room.

simulationreal robot
Chains are worse than the product · skills are not independent
\[ P(\text{DOOR}\to\text{GO-TO})\;\overset{?}{=}\;0.91\times0.98=0.89,\qquad\text{measured: }0.71\ \text{(sim)} \]

How one skill ends sets up the next. After the door, the robot’s heading depends on the door angle, and the target can be out of view. In 3 of 5 failed real CROUCH→GO-TO→PUSH runs, the crouch ended facing away from the box.

HALO’s settingvariant

Lessons from the robot

  • Frozen vs fine-tuned VLM. Fine-tuning made motion smoother and faster to react (a frozen VLM barely tells a person at 39° from 40°). But it then followed only people who looked like the single training human. Fix: re-render with many people made by Hunyuan3D.
  • Ignored words. A fine-tuned model learned “chair in view ⇒ sit” and ignored the command. Fix: black out the image in 30% of training samples.
  • System ID. Real motors gave 78–90% of the commanded stiffness with 25–30 ms delay. Fitting this cut joint tracking error from 26.9% to 10.1%.
  • Carpet. Feet sink 1–2 cm; a rigid-floor policy reads that as tilting and shuffles. Fix: randomize ground stiffness (1.3–6.5 kN/m) and friction.
  • What predicts real stability. The action-rate penalty did; the raw sim reward barely did. Without it, ankles and wrists buzz audibly.
Part 7

Limits

  • A person still writes each new task: its prompts and keyframes. The skill list grows at human speed.
  • No touch sensing. Once an object leaves the camera view, the policy has no sign it is still there.
  • The tracker follows the plan without knowing its goal (e.g. “the box should end up there”).
  • The orchestrator is a simple prompt loop; more skills will need a more capable agent.

For SuperMimic-DVA

HALO’s tracker is a depth-conditioned whole-body motion tracker: height-map experts distilled into a 48×84 depth student, then RL with depth in the loop. Removing depth costs 10 points on SIT (84 → 74). Its Table I claims it is the first system to pair a perceptive tracker with an onboard generated whole-body plan.

Add it next to DWP in the related-work and novelty checks.

Source: S. Hu, A. Abuduweili, Y. Meng, S. Liu, Q. Leboutet, C. Chen, M. Müller, V. Koltun, “Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation,” arXiv 2611.06908, 2026.
